berry-and-kohns-operating-room-technique.title: Berry & Kohn's Operating Room Technique: a guide for theatre students
berry-and-kohns-operating-room-technique.excerpt: What Berry & Kohn's Operating Room Technique covers, who it suits and how a Kenyan theatre student can use it without getting lost.
berry-and-kohns-operating-room-technique.content:
Berry & Kohn's Operating Room Technique is a long-standing textbook written for the operating room team, and it is the kind of reference many theatre programmes point students towards. It is big, so the skill is knowing how to read it in pieces.

A note on "review": this is a guide to what the book covers, who it suits and how to use it, based on its published scope. It is not a claim that I have read every page, and editions change, so check the current edition and your own syllabus before buying.

What the book is for

It is a reference for perioperative practice: the surgical environment, infection prevention, the roles of the team, patient care and safety, instruments and supplies, and a large section on how common procedures are set up. It is written with an international (largely North American) hospital in mind, so brand names and some routines will differ from what you see in Kenya.

That is not a weakness if you read it for principles. The reasons behind a sterile field, a count or a positioning rule do not change at the border.

How to read it as a student

Do not read it cover to cover. Pick the chapter that matches what your class or attachment is dealing with this week, read the headings first, then the summaries and tables, then the detail.

  • Before attachment: asepsis, the sterile field, roles and communication.
  • Before a practical: set-up, draping, counts and instrument handling.
  • Before a ward round or case: the procedure section for that specialty.

Where it will not match your hospital

Equipment, packaging, tray names and some policies differ. When the book and your preceptor disagree, ask why. Often both are acceptable, or the hospital has a policy for a reason. Write the local version in the margin of your notes.

Pairing it with other resources

Use it alongside your college notes and a good anatomy text, and check the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist yourself so you know the global baseline. A pocket procedure card of your own, built from the book, is worth more than any highlighted page.

Quick revision points

  • Use it as a reference, not a novel.
  • Read headings, tables and summaries before detail.
  • Expect brand and policy differences from Kenyan hospitals.
  • Make your own one-page set-up cards from it.
  • Ask your preceptor when practice and text differ.

Sources and links

  • WHO Surgical Safety Checklist

alexanders-surgical-procedures-review.title: Alexander's Surgical Procedures: who it is for and how to use it
alexanders-surgical-procedures-review.excerpt: A guide to Alexander's Surgical Procedures: a procedure-by-procedure reference for people who set up, assist and prepare for surgery.
alexanders-surgical-procedures-review.content:
Alexander's Surgical Procedures belongs to the Alexander family of perioperative texts and is organised around procedures rather than general theory. It answers the question every student asks the night before a new case: what actually happens, in what order, and what will be needed?

A note on "review": this is a guide to what the book covers, who it suits and how to use it, based on its published scope. It is not a claim that I have read every page, and editions change, so check the current edition and your own syllabus before buying.

What it offers

A procedure book typically explains the relevant anatomy, why the operation is done, the patient preparation and position, the equipment and supplies, the main steps and the common risks. Reading it before a case turns a confusing hour into something you can follow.

A study routine that works

Before an unfamiliar case:

  • Read the anatomy paragraph and sketch the area.
  • Write the likely instruments in the order you expect to need them.
  • Note the position, the skin prep area and the drapes.
  • After the case, correct your list with what you really saw.

That last step builds experience faster than reading alone.

Limits to keep in mind

Surgeons have preferences and hospitals have different stocks. The book shows a typical approach, not the only one. Never treat a book list as a replacement for the surgeon's request or the hospital's tray list.

Who benefits most

Students nearing attachment, new graduates preparing for a first theatre job, and anyone teaching others how to prepare. If you only buy one procedural reference, ask your lecturers which they use so your notes line up with your exams.

Quick revision points

  • Procedure books explain the why and the order of an operation.
  • Sketch the anatomy before reading steps.
  • Predict your instrument list, then correct it after the case.
  • Surgeon preference and local stock always come first.
  • Ask which edition your college recommends.

surgical-technology-for-the-surgical-tec.title: Surgical Technology for the Surgical Technologist: guide for students
surgical-technology-for-the-surgical-tec.excerpt: What the AST's core surgical technology textbook covers, and how its approach compares with theatre technology training in Kenya.
surgical-technology-for-the-surgical-tec.content:
Surgical Technology for the Surgical Technologist is the textbook associated with the Association of Surgical Technologists (AST), the US professional body for surgical technologists. If you search for resources on theatre technology outside Kenya, you will meet this book often.

A note on "review": this is a guide to what the book covers, who it suits and how to use it, based on its published scope. It is not a claim that I have read every page, and editions change, so check the current edition and your own syllabus before buying.

Why it is relevant to Kenyan students

Surgical technologist, theatre technologist and operating room technician are related titles used in different countries. The core duties overlap: preparing the theatre, maintaining the sterile field, handling instruments and supporting the surgical team. Your Kenyan scope of practice and registration may differ, so use the book for technique and principles, not as a legal description of your role.

Typical content

  • Professional and ethical foundations of the role.
  • Basic sciences relevant to surgery.
  • Infection prevention, sterilisation and aseptic technique.
  • The operating room environment and equipment.
  • Case preparation, counts and handling of specimens.
  • Procedures grouped by specialty.

Reading with a Kenyan lens

Highlight the principles that apply anywhere and put a question mark by anything that depends on US law or supply. Then compare with your college notes and your attachment hospital's policy.

Related organisation

The AST publishes standards and runs student and professional membership for its members. You can read about it on its website.

Quick revision points

  • Same core duties, different titles in different countries.
  • Use it for principles of technique and safety.
  • Do not treat foreign scope of practice as Kenyan law.
  • Mark what is local policy and ask about it.
  • Pair it with your college's own notes.

Sources and links

  • Association of Surgical Technologists

fullers-surgical-technology-principles-a.title: Fuller's Surgical Technology: Principles and Practice, a student guide
fullers-surgical-technology-principles-a.excerpt: A guide to Fuller's Surgical Technology: Principles and Practice and how to study from a large textbook in short, useful sessions.
fullers-surgical-technology-principles-a.content:
Fuller's Surgical Technology: Principles and Practice is a comprehensive text used on surgical technology programmes. Its strengths are structure and clarity, which makes it good for self-study if you have a plan.

A note on "review": this is a guide to what the book covers, who it suits and how to use it, based on its published scope. It is not a claim that I have read every page, and editions change, so check the current edition and your own syllabus before buying.

The layout helps you

Textbooks like this usually open each chapter with objectives and key terms and close with review questions. Those are free study tools. Read the objectives first so you know what you must be able to do by the end.

A weekly plan

  • Monday: skim two chapters, list the key terms.
  • Midweek: read one chapter properly and make a one-page summary.
  • Friday: close the book and answer the review questions.
  • Weekend: explain the chapter aloud to a classmate or to your phone camera.

Spacing the reading over days beats one long session.

Using the questions properly

Answer review questions without looking, then mark yourself. The wrong answers are your real study list. Move them to flashcards.

Check the match with your syllabus

A foreign text will cover topics your exam does not and skip some that it does. Use your syllabus or the past papers as the filter, and use the book to deepen those topics.

Quick revision points

  • Read objectives and key terms before the chapter.
  • Spread reading across the week.
  • Answer review questions closed-book.
  • Turn wrong answers into flashcards.
  • Filter by your own syllabus.

grays-anatomy-for-students-guide.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students: how to use it for theatre and clinical courses
grays-anatomy-for-students-guide.excerpt: A practical guide to Gray's Anatomy for Students for health students: what it offers, its clinical boxes and how not to drown in detail.
grays-anatomy-for-students-guide.content:
Gray's Anatomy for Students is a regional anatomy textbook written with learners in mind, using clinical boxes to tie structure to practice. For theatre and clinical students it is a good second-year-and-beyond reference, though it goes deeper than many diploma exams require.

A note on "review": this is a guide to what the book covers, who it suits and how to use it, based on its published scope. It is not a claim that I have read every page, and editions change, so check the current edition and your own syllabus before buying.

Regional approach

It is organised by region (for example the abdomen or the upper limb) rather than by system. That suits surgery because operations happen in regions and layers. When you read about the abdominal wall, picture the incision layers you will see in theatre.

Make the detail manageable

  • Learn the big structures and their relations first.
  • Learn nerves and vessels by what they supply and where they run.
  • Leave rare variants until the basics are secure.

If your exam is a diploma-level paper, check the past papers to see the depth expected.

Clinical boxes

Short boxes link anatomy to injuries, procedures and common problems. They are the best part for retention because they give each structure a reason to matter.

Pairing with an atlas

Use an atlas of illustrations for pictures and this book for explanation. Quick sketches of your own are what make the knowledge stick.

Quick revision points

  • Study by region and layer, as surgeons see it.
  • Learn big structures and relations first.
  • Read the clinical boxes: they make facts memorable.
  • Check your past papers for the depth you need.
  • Draw from memory, then compare.

netters-atlas-of-human-anatomy-how-to-st.title: Netter's Atlas of Human Anatomy: how to study with an atlas
netters-atlas-of-human-anatomy-how-to-st.excerpt: An atlas shows you what things look like; it does not teach on its own. Here is how to study anatomy properly with Netter's Atlas of Human Anatomy.
netters-atlas-of-human-anatomy-how-to-st.content:
Netter's Atlas of Human Anatomy is known for its clear, painted illustrations that show structures the way a surgeon might see them. Many health programmes recommend an atlas like it alongside a text.

A note on "review": this is a guide to what the book covers, who it suits and how to use it, based on its published scope. It is not a claim that I have read every page, and editions change, so check the current edition and your own syllabus before buying.

Why illustrations matter

Anatomy is three-dimensional. A good plate shows relations that long paragraphs struggle to describe, such as what lies in front of what, and where a nerve passes a bone.

The cover-and-recall method

Study a plate for a minute. Cover the labels with paper. Name each structure aloud or on paper. Check, then repeat only the ones you missed. This is active recall, and it is far better than rereading.

Tie pictures to function

After naming a structure, say what it does and what happens if it is injured. One sentence is enough. This builds the clinical link examiners and surgeons care about.

Practical tips

  • Use one region per session.
  • Trace and colour your own simplified version of a plate for personal study.
  • The aim is to be able to draw it from memory, not just recognise it.
  • Share your sketches with a study partner for correction.

Quick revision points

  • An atlas is for pictures; pair it with a text for explanation.
  • Use cover-and-recall, not rereading.
  • Add one sentence of function for each structure.
  • One region per session.
  • Redraw from memory to test yourself.

guyton-and-hall-physiology-how-to-read-w.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology: reading without burnout
guyton-and-hall-physiology-how-to-read-w.excerpt: Guyton and Hall is a classic physiology text. Here is how to extract what you need for a health diploma or degree without reading 1,000 pages.
guyton-and-hall-physiology-how-to-read-w.content:
Guyton and Hall's Textbook of Medical Physiology is one of the most widely used physiology references in medical education. It is detailed and has many diagrams of control systems.

A note on "review": this is a guide to what the book covers, who it suits and how to use it, based on its published scope. It is not a claim that I have read every page, and editions change, so check the current edition and your own syllabus before buying.

Read for understanding

Physiology is about how the body keeps things stable. For each system ask: what is being controlled, what senses it, what responds, and what goes wrong. That four-question frame keeps you from memorising lists.

Ranges and pathways

Learn the normal ranges for vital signs and common blood values (check them in your own syllabus), and learn pathways as flowcharts you can redraw.

Link to theatre

Anaesthesia and surgery change breathing, circulation, temperature and fluid balance. Knowing the normal state lets you notice and describe the abnormal one.

How to avoid burnout

Pick one system a week. Read the introduction and summary, then the sections your syllabus lists. Make a one-page summary with a diagram. Revisit after three days and again after a week.

Quick revision points

  • Ask what is controlled, sensed and corrected.
  • Redraw pathways as simple flowcharts.
  • Know normal ranges from your syllabus.
  • Connect each system to anaesthesia and surgery.
  • One system and one summary page per week.

bailey-and-loves-short-practice-of-surge.title: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery: a guide for non-surgeons
bailey-and-loves-short-practice-of-surge.excerpt: Bailey & Love is a surgical classic. Here is how a theatre technology student can use it to understand the operations they set up for.
bailey-and-loves-short-practice-of-surge.content:
Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery is a standard text for surgical trainees and medical students. It is written for people who will decide on and perform surgery, so it goes beyond what a theatre technologist must know, but small, targeted reading pays off.

A note on "review": this is a guide to what the book covers, who it suits and how to use it, based on its published scope. It is not a claim that I have read every page, and editions change, so check the current edition and your own syllabus before buying.

Why a theatre technologist might read it

Knowing why an operation is done, and what can go wrong, helps you anticipate needs and understand urgency. When a case turns into an emergency, the person who understands the condition is the person who reacts calmly.

What to read and what to skip

Read the sections on conditions you commonly see: hernias, appendicitis, caesarean section related surgery (in the obstetric texts), fractures and wounds. Skip the decision-making detail and focus on anatomy, steps and complications.

Make quick cards

For each operation create a card: indication, position, incision, key structures at risk, usual instruments, common complications. Compare with what you see in theatre.

Be clear about scope

Reading surgical texts does not change your scope of practice. It improves understanding and teamwork.

Quick revision points

  • Understanding the condition helps you anticipate needs.
  • Focus on common operations first.
  • Make a card per operation.
  • Compare cards with real cases.
  • Reading widely does not change your scope of practice.

oxford-handbook-of-clinical-surgery-pock.title: Oxford Handbook of Clinical Surgery: a pocket reference guide
oxford-handbook-of-clinical-surgery-pock.excerpt: A guide to the Oxford Handbook style of pocket reference for surgery: what it is good for, and what a pocket book cannot replace.
oxford-handbook-of-clinical-surgery-pock.content:
The Oxford Handbook of Clinical Surgery is part of a well-known series of compact clinical handbooks. Handbooks are written to be carried and used on the ward, and students often use them for fast revision.

A note on "review": this is a guide to what the book covers, who it suits and how to use it, based on its published scope. It is not a claim that I have read every page, and editions change, so check the current edition and your own syllabus before buying.

Strengths of a handbook

Compact layout, bullet points, diagrams and lists make it useful for last-minute review, ward preparation and recalling the structure of a topic.

Limits

Because it is short it leaves out the reasoning. If something is unclear, go to a full textbook or ask a lecturer. Do not learn only from the handbook, or you will have lists without understanding.

How to use it

  • Read the relevant page before a ward round or a case.
  • Use it to check the order of steps, not to decide treatment.
  • Add your own notes in the margins for local practice.

Edition and local practice

Always check you have a recent edition and that local protocols, for example drug names and doses in Kenya, are confirmed with your hospital guidelines.

Quick revision points

  • Handbooks are for quick recall, not deep learning.
  • Pair with a full textbook for reasoning.
  • Do not use a handbook to decide treatment.
  • Check the edition date.
  • Confirm local protocols with hospital guidelines.

kumar-and-clarks-clinical-medicine-guide.title: Kumar & Clark's Clinical Medicine: using it as a student
kumar-and-clarks-clinical-medicine-guide.excerpt: A guide to Kumar & Clark's Clinical Medicine, a reference on diseases, presentation and management used widely in Africa and beyond.
kumar-and-clarks-clinical-medicine-guide.content:
Kumar & Clark's Clinical Medicine is a common reference on internal medicine. It is popular in many countries, including Kenya, and is often recommended for clinical students.

A note on "review": this is a guide to what the book covers, who it suits and how to use it, based on its published scope. It is not a claim that I have read every page, and editions change, so check the current edition and your own syllabus before buying.

Why it matters to theatre students

Patients who come to theatre have other conditions: diabetes, hypertension, asthma, heart disease, HIV, anaemia. Understanding these helps you understand why anaesthesia teams ask the questions they do and why some cases are riskier.

A reading template

For each disease write five lines: cause, how it presents, how it is confirmed, main treatment, and complications. Add one line: what does it mean for surgery?

Focus on common conditions

Start with those you see most on the ward and in pre-operative lists. Learn the red flags and the normal ranges.

Know your limits

Clinical reference books describe medical management. Theatre staff do not prescribe or change treatment; use the knowledge to communicate clearly and escalate properly.

Quick revision points

  • Patients in theatre often have medical conditions.
  • Use a five-line template per disease.
  • Start with the common conditions.
  • Learn red flags and when to escalate.
  • Knowledge supports communication, not prescribing.

the-checklist-manifesto-what-theatre-sta.title: The Checklist Manifesto by Atul Gawande: what theatre staff can learn
the-checklist-manifesto-what-theatre-sta.excerpt: Atul Gawande's The Checklist Manifesto is about why simple checklists save lives and why people resist them. A guide to the ideas for theatre teams.
the-checklist-manifesto-what-theatre-sta.content:
The Checklist Manifesto is a popular book by surgeon and writer Atul Gawande about how checklists reduce errors in complex work, drawing on examples from aviation, construction and medicine. It is closely tied to the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist.

A note on "review": this is a guide to what the book covers, who it suits and how to use it, based on its published scope. It is not a claim that I have read every page, and editions change, so check the current edition and your own syllabus before buying.

The main argument

In complex jobs, experts still forget steps. A good checklist does not replace skill; it protects against the predictable slips: the forgotten allergy check, the missing instrument count, the antibiotic not given.

Why it matters in theatre

The WHO Surgical Safety Checklist, introduced to reduce avoidable surgical harm, is built around pauses before anaesthesia, before incision and before the patient leaves theatre. The book explains the thinking behind this approach.

What makes a checklist work

  • It is short and uses plain wording.
  • It is used at natural pause points.
  • The whole team takes part, and anyone can speak up.
  • It is tested in practice and revised.

What to take from it as a student

Treat the checklist as a team conversation, not paperwork. When you are the junior, asking one clear question aloud can be the most important thing you do in a case. Read the checklist itself on the WHO page.

Quick revision points

  • Checklists protect against predictable slips.
  • They work best at pause points.
  • Everyone in the team must be able to speak up.
  • A checklist is a conversation, not a tick-box.
  • Read the WHO checklist yourself.

make-it-stick-learning-science-for-stude.title: Make It Stick: the learning science every health student should know
make-it-stick-learning-science-for-stude.excerpt: Make It Stick explains why retrieval, spacing and interleaving beat rereading. A guide to the book's ideas, applied to Kenyan health students.
make-it-stick-learning-science-for-stude.content:
Make It Stick: The Science of Successful Learning, by Peter Brown, Henry Roediger and Mark McDaniel, summarises research on how people actually learn. It is one of the most useful non-medical books for any student.

A note on "review": this is a guide to what the book covers, who it suits and how to use it, based on its published scope. It is not a claim that I have read every page, and editions change, so check the current edition and your own syllabus before buying.

The central idea

Learning feels easy when you reread and highlight, but that feeling is misleading. Learning that lasts usually feels harder: you try to recall without looking, you space sessions out, and you mix problem types.

Applying it to exams

  • Retrieval practice: close your notes and write what you remember.
  • Spacing: revisit a topic after a day, a week and a month.
  • Interleaving: mix topics in one session instead of one long block.
  • Elaboration: explain how a fact connects to others.
  • Reflection: study your errors.

A theatre example

Learning the instrument families: cover the names and recall by picture, then by function; return after two days and mix them with sterilisation questions.

Why I recommend it

It changes how you study without needing money or equipment. You can read the principles in a weekend and use them for a career.

Quick revision points

  • Rereading is weak; retrieval is strong.
  • Space sessions out.
  • Mix topics rather than blocking.
  • Explain ideas in your own words.
  • Use mistakes as your study guide.

a-mind-for-numbers-and-learning-how-to-l.title: A Mind for Numbers: takeaways for health students
a-mind-for-numbers-and-learning-how-to-l.excerpt: Barbara Oakley's A Mind for Numbers is aimed at maths and science learners. Here are the ideas that help health students most.
a-mind-for-numbers-and-learning-how-to-l.content:
A Mind for Numbers: How to Excel at Math and Science (Even If You Flunked Algebra) by Barbara Oakley is a popular learning guide. Its ideas are useful for anatomy, physiology and any subject that feels heavy.

A note on "review": this is a guide to what the book covers, who it suits and how to use it, based on its published scope. It is not a claim that I have read every page, and editions change, so check the current edition and your own syllabus before buying.

Two modes of thinking

The book describes a focused mode, where you concentrate, and a diffuse mode, where the mind wanders and often connects ideas. Alternating them helps: work hard for a short period, take a real break, then return.

Chunking

A chunk is a piece of knowledge you can use as one unit. Learning a chunk takes understanding, practice and context. Practise one clinical procedure until the steps feel like one thing, then move on.

Practical routines

  • Use short timed study blocks with real breaks.
  • Start on the hardest topic when you are fresh.
  • Test yourself regularly.
  • Sleep and exercise count as study tools.

Procrastination

The book also covers procrastination and how starting for just a few minutes can break the avoidance habit.

Quick revision points

  • Alternate focused work with rest.
  • Build chunks you can use as units.
  • Test yourself and repeat the hard parts.
  • Hard topic first, while you are fresh.
  • Sleep is part of studying.

atomic-habits-for-students-and-content-c.title: Atomic Habits for students and content creators: key ideas
atomic-habits-for-students-and-content-c.excerpt: James Clear's Atomic Habits is about small changes that compound. A guide to using its ideas for study routines and posting schedules.
atomic-habits-for-students-and-content-c.content:
Atomic Habits by James Clear argues that small, consistent actions matter more than big, occasional efforts. It is not a medical book, but it applies directly to study, work and content creation.

A note on "review": this is a guide to what the book covers, who it suits and how to use it, based on its published scope. It is not a claim that I have read every page, and editions change, so check the current edition and your own syllabus before buying.

The four ideas

Make the habit obvious, attractive, easy and satisfying. For breaking a habit, invert each: make it invisible, unattractive, difficult and unsatisfying.

Example: a revision habit

Cue: after supper, the notes are already on the desk. Easy: start with five minutes. Satisfying: tick a calendar. Identity: I am a person who studies a little every day.

Example: a posting habit

Keep a list of topics so there is always the next idea. Make the first step tiny, such as writing the title. Track streaks if that motivates you, but do not punish yourself for a missed day.

Caution

A book cannot do the work for you. Pick one habit, run it for a month and adjust.

Quick revision points

  • Small actions compound.
  • Make good habits obvious and easy.
  • Start with five minutes.
  • Track progress visibly.
  • Pick one habit at a time.

deep-work-for-health-students-focus-in-a.title: Deep Work for health students: focus in a phone-filled world
deep-work-for-health-students-focus-in-a.excerpt: Cal Newport's Deep Work is about sustained focus. A guide to using the idea for revision when phones and WhatsApp keep pulling you away.
deep-work-for-health-students-focus-in-a.content:
Deep Work by Cal Newport argues that the ability to focus without distraction is increasingly valuable. For students, it means protecting some blocks of time for hard thinking.

A note on "review": this is a guide to what the book covers, who it suits and how to use it, based on its published scope. It is not a claim that I have read every page, and editions change, so check the current edition and your own syllabus before buying.

What counts as deep work

Tasks that need full concentration: understanding a hard chapter, writing an essay, solving practice questions. Shallow work such as replying to messages is fine but should not fill the day.

A student routine

  • Pick a one- or two-hour block.
  • Put the phone in another room or on aeroplane mode.
  • Decide a clear target, such as 'finish the cardiac cycle summary'.
  • Take a break, then stop for the day when it ends.

When life is not quiet

In a shared home or a hostel, silence is not guaranteed. Use headphones, the library, or an early morning slot. Even one good block a day adds up.

Balance

Deep work is not a reason to ignore people. Tell family or friends when you are studying and when you will be free.

Quick revision points

  • Protect blocks for hard thinking.
  • Phone out of reach during study.
  • Set a clear target for each block.
  • Use the quietest time you can find.
  • Stop on time and rest.

where-there-is-no-doctor-community-healt.excerpt: Hesperian's Where There Is No Doctor is a practical health book for communities with limited services. What it offers, and its limits.
where-there-is-no-doctor-community-healt.content:
Where There Is No Doctor by David Werner and colleagues, published by Hesperian Health Guides, is a village health care handbook written in plain language and used in many countries. Hesperian makes many of its guides available for free online.

A note on "review": this is a guide to what the book covers, who it suits and how to use it, based on its published scope. It is not a claim that I have read every page, and editions change, so check the current edition and your own syllabus before buying.

Why it is useful

It shows how to explain common problems clearly, how to recognise danger signs and when to send someone to a health facility. Content creators can learn from its style: short, direct and focused on action.

What it is not

It is not a substitute for a clinician, and treatment advice changes. Always confirm with current Kenyan guidelines and a health worker.

Lessons for health educators

  • Use plain words and clear pictures.
  • Say what to do, and when to go to hospital.
  • Respect local context and resources.
  • Avoid fear; give people confidence to act.

Where to find it

Search for Hesperian Health Guides on their official website for the current free resources.

Quick revision points

  • Plain language is a skill to practise.
  • Always include when to seek help.
  • Do not replace professional care.
  • Check advice against current local guidelines.
  • Use pictures and short steps.

anatomy-and-physiology-textbooks-tortora.title: Tortora vs Marieb: choosing an anatomy and physiology textbook
anatomy-and-physiology-textbooks-tortora.excerpt: Two widely used anatomy and physiology textbooks compared by how they teach, so you can choose one that suits you.
anatomy-and-physiology-textbooks-tortora.content:
Principles of Anatomy and Physiology (Tortora and Derrickson) and Human Anatomy & Physiology (Marieb and Hoehn) are two of the most commonly used introductory texts in health programmes worldwide. Both are good. The better one is the one you will actually read.

A note on "review": this is a guide to what the book covers, who it suits and how to use it, based on its published scope. It is not a claim that I have read every page, and editions change, so check the current edition and your own syllabus before buying.

What they share

Both combine anatomy and physiology, include colour diagrams, clinical applications and review questions, and are designed for first-year health students.

How to choose

  • Compare the table of contents with your syllabus.
  • Read the same topic in both and see which explanation you follow.
  • Look at the diagrams and end-of-chapter questions.
  • Check whether an older edition is acceptable for your course; asking your lecturer can save money.

Where to find them

College libraries often hold copies. Ask lecturers if previous editions are fine for your course.

A caution about copies

Buying legitimate copies supports authors. Many publishers offer low-cost student editions or library access.

Quick revision points

  • Choose by your syllabus and how you learn.
  • Sample the same topic in both.
  • Ask whether an older edition is acceptable.
  • Use library copies where you can.
  • Do not rely on photocopies of random pages.

the-language-of-medicine-medical-termino.title: The Language of Medicine: a guide to learning medical terminology from a book
the-language-of-medicine-medical-termino.excerpt: Davi-Ellen Chabner's The Language of Medicine teaches terminology through word parts. How to use that approach to learn faster.
the-language-of-medicine-medical-termino.content:
The Language of Medicine by Davi-Ellen Chabner is a textbook that teaches medical terminology by breaking terms into roots, prefixes and suffixes. This approach lets you work out new words instead of memorising each one.

A note on "review": this is a guide to what the book covers, who it suits and how to use it, based on its published scope. It is not a claim that I have read every page, and editions change, so check the current edition and your own syllabus before buying.

Why word parts work

Hepat- means liver, -itis means inflammation, so hepatitis is liver inflammation. Once you learn a few hundred parts, thousands of terms become guessable.

How to study

  • Learn 10 word parts a day.
  • Build five terms from them.
  • Say each term aloud for pronunciation.
  • Review with flashcards after two days.

In theatre

You will meet words like appendicectomy, laparotomy, cholecystectomy and tracheostomy. Break them apart and the names of operations explain themselves.

See also

My post on prefixes and suffixes gives a quick start before you commit to a full book.

Quick revision points

  • Learn word parts, not single words.
  • Build new terms from known parts.
  • Say words aloud.
  • Review with spaced flashcards.
  • Operation names are built from parts.

when-breath-becomes-air-and-being-mortal.title: Two books for health workers: When Breath Becomes Air and Being Mortal
when-breath-becomes-air-and-being-mortal.excerpt: Two widely read books about illness, death and what matters in care, and why future health workers should read them.
when-breath-becomes-air-and-being-mortal.content:
When Breath Becomes Air by Paul Kalanithi and Being Mortal by Atul Gawande are two well-known books that look at serious illness from the inside. They are not study guides. They are reminders of why the work matters.

A note on "review": this is a guide to what the book covers, who it suits and how to use it, based on its published scope. It is not a claim that I have read every page, and editions change, so check the current edition and your own syllabus before buying.

When Breath Becomes Air

A neurosurgeon-in-training writes about becoming a patient himself. It is about identity, purpose and how a doctor's view changes when he is on the other side of the bed.

Being Mortal

Gawande, a surgeon, argues that modern medicine can focus too much on survival and too little on a person's priorities in serious illness or old age. It encourages honest conversations.

What a theatre student can take from them

  • Patients are people with fears and values.
  • Clear, kind communication matters.
  • Small acts of respect (a name, a blanket, a calm voice) are part of care.
  • The best technical skill still sits inside a human relationship.

A caution

Both books touch death and grief. Read them when you have the emotional space, and talk to someone you trust if they bring up difficult feelings.

Quick revision points

  • Patients are people first.
  • Honest communication is a skill.
  • Small kindnesses matter in theatre.
  • Read when you have the emotional space.
  • These books inform your attitude, not your exam.

Ask first

Ask your lecturers which text the exams follow, and ask seniors who did well which books they actually used. Their answer is often more modest than the reading list.

Check the match

Open the table of contents and compare it with your syllabus. A book that covers 70% of your course well is better than one that covers 100% badly.

Sample before you buy

Read one chapter in the library or from a classmate. If you follow it easily, it is a good fit.

Priorities

  • A core anatomy and physiology text.
  • A theatre or clinical practice reference from your syllabus.
  • A pocket handbook for revision.
  • A good dictionary of medical terms.

Buy one at a time, and use your notes to fill gaps.

Digital or print

Print helps with annotation and exam preparation; digital is cheaper and searchable. Choose based on how you study.

Quick revision points

  • Ask lecturers and successful seniors.
  • Match the contents to your syllabus.
  • Sample before buying.
  • Buy in priority order, one at a time.
  • Use libraries and legal digital copies.

what-is-kmtc-and-how-it-fits-in-kenyas-h.excerpt: A plain explanation of the Kenya Medical Training College (KMTC): what it is, the kinds of programmes it runs and how to check its current course list.
what-is-kmtc-and-how-it-fits-in-kenyas-h.content:
If you want a career in health in Kenya, you will hear "KMTC" within the first week. The Kenya Medical Training College is the country's best-known public institution for training mid-level health workers.

What it is

KMTC is a public institution that trains health professionals across Kenya. It is run under the Ministry of Health framework and has campuses in many counties. It runs programmes at different levels, commonly certificate, diploma and some higher qualifications, in areas such as nursing, clinical medicine, medical laboratory, pharmacy, public health, physiotherapy and others.

Why people choose it

  • It is a long-established, well-known name.
  • Fees are usually lower than many private colleges, though they differ by programme and change over time.
  • Graduates are widely recognised by employers.
  • It has campuses in many parts of the country, so a student may train closer to home.

What to confirm yourself

Course lists, entry requirements, intake months, fees and campus offerings change. The only safe source is the official KMTC website and its current admission notices. Do not rely on old PDFs, social media posts or agents.

Where this blog fits

I am a perioperative theatre technology graduate, not a KMTC spokesperson. These posts explain how to research and compare; always verify the current details with KMTC directly.

Quick revision points

  • KMTC is Kenya's best-known public health training college.
  • It offers many programmes at different levels.
  • Fees, intakes and offerings change.
  • Use the official KMTC website for current information.
  • Avoid agents and unofficial lists.

how-to-apply-to-kmtc-step-by-step-checkl.excerpt: A checklist for applying to KMTC or any public health college: documents, deadlines, mistakes to avoid, and what to do after applying.
how-to-apply-to-kmtc-step-by-step-checkl.content:
Applications are won or lost on small things: a missing document, a wrong subject, a missed date. This checklist is general; the official KMTC instructions always override it.

1. Choose a course you qualify for

Read the entry requirements for your chosen programme on the official website. Check the mean grade and the specific subjects, such as biology, chemistry, mathematics or English/Kiswahili where required.

2. Get documents ready

  • KCSE result slip or certificate.
  • National ID or birth certificate.
  • Passport photos if asked.
  • Any previous certificates for upgrading routes.

Scan them clearly in advance.

3. Apply only through official channels

Use the KMTC website and its stated application system. Be careful with fake sites and social media pages that look official. Never pay an individual who promises "guaranteed admission".

4. Watch deadlines

Intakes are announced on the official site. Set reminders instead of waiting for friends.

5. After applying

Save your confirmation, keep your phone and email active and check the official notices for selection lists. If you are not selected, look at alternative courses or other accredited colleges, and consider the next intake.

Quick revision points

  • Check entry requirements first.
  • Prepare scanned documents early.
  • Apply through the official system only.
  • Never pay for guaranteed admission.
  • Keep checking official notices.

One reason students feel lost is that nobody explains levels. Here is a simple map.

The basic ladder

  • Certificate: shorter, practical entry-level training for support roles.
  • Diploma: the main professional training for many mid-level health cadres.
  • Higher diploma or bachelor's: deeper study, often for leadership, teaching or specialisation.
  • Master's and beyond: advanced and research-oriented study.

How each profession fits depends on its regulator and training standards.

Why levels matter

Employers and regulators look at the level and the institution. Your qualification determines which roles you can apply for and what upgrading routes exist.

The KNQA framework

The Kenya National Qualifications Authority coordinates the national qualifications framework and can help with questions about recognition and alignment of qualifications.

Planning an upgrade

Check whether a diploma gets credit transfer into a degree, and what experience or bridging courses are required. Ask the university before you pay for anything.

Quick revision points

  • Certificate, diploma and degree are different levels.
  • The level affects jobs and upgrading routes.
  • KNQA helps with qualification recognition.
  • Ask universities about credit transfer.
  • Plan the path before enrolling.

does-kmtc-offer-perioperative-theatre-te.title: Does KMTC offer perioperative theatre technology? How to check
does-kmtc-offer-perioperative-theatre-te.excerpt: Online guides disagree about whether KMTC offers perioperative theatre technology. Here is how to check the current position yourself.
does-kmtc-offer-perioperative-theatre-te.content:
Search for perioperative theatre technology and you will find articles with different answers about which colleges offer it. One widely read guide, last updated in 2025, says KMTC is not currently offering the diploma or certificate, but it does not cite a source or date for the claim.

Why I will not give you a yes or no

Course lists change between intakes, and I do not have access to KMTC's current admissions system. Giving you a confident answer from a blog would be irresponsible.

How to check the current position

  • Open the official KMTC website and look at the current programmes list and admission notice.
  • Search for the exact course name and for "theatre" variants.
  • If it is not listed, email or call the registrar and ask in writing.
  • Save the reply with the date.

If KMTC does not offer it

Other accredited institutions train theatre technologists. See my post on where the course is offered and how to verify the institution.

A caution about names

Programmes can have similar names, such as theatre nursing, which is a different qualification from theatre technology. Make sure you are comparing the same thing.

  • Guides online disagree; verify the current position.
  • Use KMTC's official programme list.
  • Ask the registrar in writing.
  • Do not mix up theatre nursing and theatre technology.
  • Save the answer with the date.

I trained in perioperative theatre technology, so I get asked this weekly. The honest answer is that offerings change, and a list in a blog is only a starting point.

  • Visit each college's own website or call.
  • Confirm the course name, level and intake.
  • Verify accreditation and registration (see my post on how to verify a college).
  • Ask which hospital trains students in theatre.
  • Speak to current students or recent graduates.

What matters more than the name

Clinical placement quality, supervision, a functioning skills lab and a clear route to professional recognition.

When to avoid

Walk away from any college that cannot show current accreditation or gives vague answers about attachment.

  • Public lists are starting points, not endorsements.
  • Verify course name, level and intake.
  • Check accreditation before paying.
  • Ask about theatre placement hospitals.

consolata-medical-college-theatre-techno.content:
This post is an example of how to read a college page critically, using the public page for the perioperative theatre technology course at Sister Leonella Consolata Medical College. It is not an endorsement.

What the page describes

The course page describes training to support a hospital operating theatre, including care for patients in recovery. It lists a diploma of about two and a half years and a certificate of about one year. The topics include preparing the operating room for surgery, sterilising equipment, caring for clients in theatre and testing and maintaining equipment. The diploma adds administrative and managerial duties.

The conflict you should notice

Different parts of the same site list different entry requirements and intake months. One part gives KCSE C- for the diploma and D for the certificate; another lists C and C- respectively. Intakes are also listed differently.

What to do when a page conflicts with itself

  • Contact the college and ask for the current requirements in writing.
  • Ask for the admission letter template and fee structure.
  • Confirm accreditation independently.
  • Keep screenshots with dates.

Lesson

Read every college page this way. A single inconsistent page is not a scandal, but it is a reason to ask direct questions before you pay.

Quick revision points

  • Read college pages critically.
  • Note conflicting entry requirements.
  • Get requirements in writing.
  • Confirm accreditation independently.

kcse-entry-requirements-for-theatre-tech.title: KCSE entry requirements for theatre technology: what guides say and what to confirm
kcse-entry-requirements-for-theatre-tech.excerpt: Typical requirements quoted online for the diploma and certificate, why they differ, and how to confirm the one that applies to your college.
kcse-entry-requirements-for-theatre-tech.content:
Online guides often quote KCSE C- with biology for the diploma and lower grades for the certificate. Other pages quote slightly different grades. Both can be "true" for different institutions or different years.

What guides commonly say

  • Diploma: a mean grade around C- or C, with biology among the subjects taken.
  • Certificate: a mean grade around D or C-.
  • Alternative route: a certificate in the same field from a recognised institution, then progress to diploma.

Treat these as ranges, not rules.

Why they differ

Institutions set their own admission cut-offs within regulator standards, and requirements change by intake. Some pages are updated, others are not.

What to do

Ask the college for the requirement for your intake in writing. Ask whether bridging or a certificate-first route is accepted if your grade is lower.

If your grades are borderline

Consider a certificate and upgrade, or a related course, but never pay a person who "fixes" grades. Genuine admission needs genuine documents.

Quick revision points

  • Requirements vary by college and intake.
  • Biology is commonly requested.
  • A certificate can lead to a diploma.
  • Get requirements in writing.
  • Never pay for altered grades.

certificate-vs-diploma-in-theatre-techno.title: Certificate or diploma in theatre technology: which should you choose?
certificate-vs-diploma-in-theatre-techno.excerpt: The differences in length, scope and prospects between the certificate and the diploma in perioperative theatre technology, and how to decide.
certificate-vs-diploma-in-theatre-techno.content:
A common question is whether to start with the certificate. The answer depends on your grades, your budget and your plan.

What the programmes say

One college page describes the certificate as about one year, focused on theatre preparation, sterilisation, patient care and equipment testing. The diploma is described as about two and a half years and includes administrative and managerial duties.

Pros of the certificate

  • Faster and usually cheaper.
  • Gets you into the field sooner.
  • Can be a bridge to the diploma.

Pros of the diploma

  • Broader scope and deeper knowledge.
  • Often preferred by employers for fuller roles.
  • A better base for further study.

How to decide

Look at job adverts and ask employers which qualification they accept. If your grades allow, the diploma is usually the stronger long-term option; if money or grades limit you, the certificate can be a stepping stone.

Quick revision points

  • The diploma is longer and broader.
  • The certificate is a faster entry route.
  • Check what employers accept.
  • Plan the upgrade path.
  • Choose based on grades, budget and goals.

how-to-verify-a-medical-college-in-kenya.title: How to verify a medical college in Kenya before you pay a shilling
how-to-verify-a-medical-college-in-kenya.excerpt: A step-by-step method to check whether a college is real, accredited and approved for the course you want.
how-to-verify-a-medical-college-in-kenya.content:
Every year students pay fees to colleges that cannot give them what they promised. Verification takes an hour and can save years.

Step 1: Get the exact name and location

Names can be similar. Write the full legal name and campus.

Step 2: Check TVETA or CUE

Technical and vocational institutions are generally regulated by the TVET Authority, and universities by the Commission for University Education. TVETA publishes pages on accredited institutions and courses. CUE publishes information on universities and programmes.

Step 3: Check the programme, not just the college

A college may be registered but not approved for every course it advertises. Ask for the approval letter for your programme.

Step 4: Check the professional regulator

Many health cadres are regulated by councils and boards, for example the Nursing Council of Kenya or the Kenya Medical Practitioners and Dentists Council. Ask whether graduates of the programme can register or be licensed, and confirm with the regulator where applicable.

Step 5: See the place

Visit, speak to students and ask where clinical placement happens.

Quick revision points

  • Verify the college and the programme.
  • Use TVETA, CUE and professional regulators.
  • Ask for approval letters.
  • Visit the campus.
  • Never pay before verifying.

tveta-accreditation-explained-for-studen.title: TVETA accreditation explained for students
tveta-accreditation-explained-for-studen.excerpt: What the TVET Authority does, what accreditation means for a college, and how to use it as a student.
tveta-accreditation-explained-for-studen.content:
The Technical and Vocational Education and Training Authority (TVETA) regulates technical and vocational institutions in Kenya. Many middle-level health training colleges fall in its sphere, depending on their type and status.

What accreditation means

Accreditation means the institution has been assessed against standards for facilities, staff and programmes. It is different from simply being registered as a business.

How to use it

  • Visit the TVETA site and look for the accredited institutions page.
  • Search for the exact name.
  • Check whether the course you want is listed or approved.
  • Ask the college for its certificate and check the dates.

What it does not do

TVETA accreditation is not the same as professional licensing. After training, you may still need to register with a relevant professional body, where applicable.

Related bodies

TVET CDACC works on curricula and assessment for competency-based training, KNEC handles national examinations and certification, and KNQA coordinates qualification frameworks.

Quick revision points

  • TVETA accredits technical and vocational institutions.
  • Search the accredited list by exact name.
  • Accreditation is not the same as professional licensing.
  • Check the course as well as the college.
  • Other bodies handle curricula and exams.

cue-and-university-accreditation-explain.excerpt: The Commission for University Education regulates universities. Here is what that means for students of medicine, nursing and other health degrees.
cue-and-university-accreditation-explain.content:
If you plan a degree in a health field, you will deal with CUE and often with a professional regulator as well.

What CUE does

The Commission for University Education regulates and accredits universities and their academic programmes in Kenya.

What to check

  • The university is chartered or otherwise legally recognised.
  • The specific degree programme is approved.
  • The programme has a clinical training arrangement where required.
  • Graduates are eligible for registration with the relevant professional body.

Public and private

Both public and private universities train health professionals. Fees and entry routes differ. KUCCPS handles placement into government-sponsored places, while private or self-sponsored admission may be direct.

Practical tip

Ask the university for the approval status of the programme in writing, and compare it with the official information.

Quick revision points

  • CUE regulates universities and programmes.
  • Check the specific programme, not only the university.
  • Confirm professional registration eligibility.
  • Ask about clinical placement.
  • Get approval status in writing.

kuccps-placement-explained-for-health-co.title: KUCCPS placement explained for health courses
kuccps-placement-explained-for-health-co.excerpt: How the Kenya Universities and Colleges Central Placement Service ranks and places students, and how that affects competitive health courses.
kuccps-placement-explained-for-health-co.content:
KUCCPS is the state corporation that places eligible candidates into universities and colleges. For health courses, competition can be intense.

The basic idea

Candidates choose programmes. KUCCPS ranks applicants by their cluster points for that programme and places them according to each institution's approved capacity. At the release of the 2026/27 placement results, KUCCPS leadership explained that universities admit up to their capacity in order of ranking, and that no two universities have the same cut-off.

What students should do

  • Learn the cluster subjects for your target course.
  • Compare the previous year's cut-offs with your points.
  • Choose a mix of ambitious and safer options.
  • Use the revision window if you are unhappy or unplaced.

Remember

Cut-offs change every year, so last year's figures are guides, not promises.

Where to look

Use the official KUCCPS site for the application process and notices.

Quick revision points

  • KUCCPS ranks and places students by capacity.
  • Cut-offs differ between universities and years.
  • Choose a mix of ambitious and safe options.
  • Use revision windows.
  • Rely on the official site.

medicine-slots-702-and-6500-applicants-w.excerpt: Reporting on the 2026/27 university placement said about 6,500 applicants competed for 702 medicine slots. What this means for health students.
medicine-slots-702-and-6500-applicants-w.content:
News report from the 2026/27 KUCCPS placement release, as reported by The Standard. Numbers are from that report and may be revised.

What was reported

The Standard reported that the MBChB programme received about 6,500 applications for a combined 702 places across public and private universities, leaving nearly 5,800 qualified applicants without placement through the government placement system. The report also said that, in the 2025 KCSE, 1,936 candidates scored an A plain and 1,535 of them applied for medicine, and a further 3,328 medicine applicants had an A-.

What it means

Medicine is extremely competitive, even for top students. A strong grade does not guarantee a place.

Planning with this in mind

  • Apply for related courses as alternatives: clinical medicine, nursing, medical laboratory, pharmacy, physiotherapy and others.
  • Consider diploma-to-degree pathways.
  • Do not pay anyone who promises a guaranteed medicine slot.
  • Look at accredited private options only after verifying them.

A note on this article

I am summarising a news report, not official statistics. For the official position, check KUCCPS announcements.

Quick revision points

  • Medicine places are far fewer than applicants.
  • Reported: about 6,500 applicants for 702 slots.
  • Good grades still need a plan B.
  • Related courses and pathways exist.
  • Beware of anyone selling guaranteed slots.

clinical-medicine-diploma-or-degree-how-.excerpt: A comparison of the clinical medicine diploma and degree routes in Kenya in terms of length, cost, scope and next steps.
clinical-medicine-diploma-or-degree-how-.content:
Clinical officers are a major part of Kenya's health workforce. Students often ask whether to start with a diploma or aim straight for a degree.

What is on offer

A 2026 guide lists clinical medicine programmes at several universities, with annual tuition estimates ranging from roughly KES 160,000 at one private university to over KES 500,000 at another. The same guide does not state the year the figures apply, so confirm directly. Diploma programmes are also offered by medical training colleges.

Things to compare

  • Total length and total cost, not just yearly fees.
  • Entry requirements and subject clusters.
  • Where clinical rotations are done.
  • Registration and licensing with the relevant professional council.
  • Credit transfer if you start with a diploma and plan to upgrade.

Think about money

A degree can be a good long-term step, but only if you can finish it. A diploma that you complete is better than a degree you cannot afford.

Ask the regulator

Contact the relevant council to confirm registration conditions for graduates of each programme.

Quick revision points

  • Compare total cost and length.
  • Confirm registration with the regulator.
  • Check credit transfer for upgrades.
  • Finish what you can afford.
  • Fee figures vary and change.

nursing-career-pathways-in-kenya-college.content:
Nursing is one of the most common entry points into health careers, and the Nursing Council of Kenya (NCK) is the statutory regulator for nursing and midwifery.

The role of the Council

The Nursing Council of Kenya runs registration and licensing and conducts licensing examinations. Its website has an online portal and a published exam calendar.

Typical routes

Training is offered at various levels by approved institutions, including public colleges and universities. Programme names and levels evolve, so always check the current NCK requirements.

Why it matters for theatre students

Perioperative nursing and theatre technology are different professions. Nurses train in a broader field and may specialise in perioperative nursing; theatre technologists train specifically for theatre support. Understanding the difference helps you explain your role and avoid confusion.

Next steps

If you are choosing between professions, speak to practitioners and shadow if you can.

Quick revision points

  • NCK regulates nursing and midwifery.
  • Check training approval before enrolling.
  • Licensing exams follow training.
  • Perioperative nursing differs from theatre technology.
  • Shadow practitioners before choosing.

how-much-does-health-college-really-cost.title: How much does health college really cost? A budget template
how-much-does-health-college-really-cost.excerpt: Tuition is only part of the cost. A template for budgeting a health diploma or degree, with the hidden costs people forget.
how-much-does-health-college-really-cost.content:
I will not quote fees, because they differ between colleges and change. What I can give you is a way to calculate your own total.

The categories

  • Tuition and other charges listed in the fee structure.
  • Accommodation and food.
  • Transport, especially to clinical attachment sites.
  • Uniforms, shoes, name tags and basic equipment.
  • Books and printing.
  • Exams, registration and licensing fees.
  • Emergency buffer.

A simple method

Ask the college for the full fee structure and for how fees are split across terms. Add your own monthly living costs times the number of months. Add one-off costs. This gives your total and your first-term cash need.

Ways to reduce cost

Compare colleges, look at public institutions, ask about instalments, apply for HELB or bursaries where eligible and share textbooks with classmates.

Warning

Do not pay large fees to an individual or an unofficial account. Pay only to the college's official channels and keep receipts.

Quick revision points

  • Tuition is only part of total cost.
  • Ask for the full fee structure in writing.
  • Budget for attachment travel and lodging.
  • Pay only through official channels.
  • Keep every receipt.

helb-loans-and-bursaries-for-college-stu.content:
Money is the reason many good students delay or drop training. Funding exists, but you must go through legitimate channels.

HELB

The Higher Education Loans Board (HELB) is the government body that provides loans to eligible students in higher education. Check its official site for who is eligible, the application steps and the current terms, because these change.

Bursaries

Counties, constituency funds, churches, foundations and some employers offer bursaries or sponsorships. Rules, amounts and deadlines vary. Visit the local office and ask early.

Scholarships

Search for scholarships offered by the institution itself, professional bodies or NGOs. Read the terms and check they are real.

Scams

Nobody should charge you for a guaranteed bursary or HELB approval. Use only official offices and websites.

Plan the repayment

If you take a loan, understand the repayment terms and how long it will take to repay on an expected salary.

Quick revision points

  • HELB is the official government loan body.
  • Bursaries come from many local sources.
  • Apply early and keep documents ready.
  • Never pay for guaranteed funding.
  • Understand repayment before borrowing.

red-flags-of-a-fake-or-risky-medical-col.title: Red flags in a medical college advert
red-flags-of-a-fake-or-risky-medical-col.excerpt: Ten warning signs that a college advert on social media or WhatsApp may be unreliable, and what to do instead.
red-flags-of-a-fake-or-risky-medical-col.content:
Social media has made it easy to advertise. It has also made it easy to hide.

Ten red flags

  • Guaranteed admission regardless of grades.
  • Pressure to pay today or lose the slot.
  • Payment to a personal phone number or account.
  • No physical address, or one that cannot be found.
  • No evidence of accreditation or programme approval.
  • Prices far below or above others without explanation.
  • Courses with names you cannot find anywhere else.
  • No clear attachment arrangement.
  • Refusal to put terms in writing.
  • Negative reports from former students.

What to do

Verify with the regulators, visit the campus, ask for written terms and talk to current students. Share suspicious adverts with friends so others are not caught.

Report

If you believe an institution is operating illegally, report it to the relevant authority.

Not every advert is bad

Many good colleges advertise. The test is whether they can answer verification questions clearly and in writing.

Quick revision points

  • Guaranteed admission is a red flag.
  • Pressure to pay quickly is a red flag.
  • Use official channels and written terms.
  • Verify with regulators.
  • Ask students who have been there.

twenty-questions-to-ask-a-college-before.title: Twenty questions to ask a college before you pay fees
twenty-questions-to-ask-a-college-before.excerpt: A question list you can send by email or ask in person to test whether a college is organised and honest.
twenty-questions-to-ask-a-college-before.content:
Colleges with good answers usually answer quickly. Colleges that avoid questions are telling you something.

About the college

  • What is your accreditation and registration status, and can I have a copy?
  • Is this exact programme approved, and by whom?
  • Who is the principal and what is the physical address?
  • How many students are in a class?

About the programme

  • How long is it and what are the intake months?
  • What are the entry requirements in writing?
  • What practical facilities do you have (lab, skills room)?
  • Which hospitals do students attend for attachment, and who pays transport and lodging?

About cost

  • Are there extra costs such as exams, uniforms and attachment fees?

  • Which account do I pay into, in the college's name?

About outcomes

  • Can graduates register or be licensed with the relevant body?
  • How many graduates were employed or placed last year?
  • Can I speak to a recent graduate?
  • How are complaints handled?

clinical-attachment-what-a-good-college-.title: Clinical attachment: what a good college should arrange for you
clinical-attachment-what-a-good-college-.excerpt: Attachment is where you become competent. Here is what to expect a college to organise, and what to do if it does not.
clinical-attachment-what-a-good-college-.content:
Good clinical attachment can make you employable. Poor attachment can leave you with a certificate and little confidence.

What a college should provide

  • A confirmed attachment site and dates.
  • A list of competencies you must achieve.
  • A logbook and clear assessment method.
  • A supervisor from the hospital and a link person at the college.
  • Guidance on conduct, uniforms and safety.

What to arrange yourself

Transport, accommodation, uniforms, personal protective equipment where not provided, and any vaccinations the hospital requires.

My own experience

My attachment at Likuyani Sub-County Hospital between February and April 2024 included theatre setup and turnover, CSSD sterilisation and the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist. The lesson was to ask questions, do the basics well and record what I learned every day.

If things go wrong

Write down what is happening, speak to your supervisor politely, and escalate to the college's link person if needed.

Quick revision points

  • Attachment needs a confirmed site and plan.
  • Keep a daily logbook.
  • Know your supervisor and link person.
  • Arrange transport and lodging early.
  • Escalate problems politely and early.

kcse-subjects-and-cluster-points-for-hea.title: KCSE subjects and cluster points for health courses, explained simply
kcse-subjects-and-cluster-points-for-hea.excerpt: What cluster subjects are, why biology and chemistry matter for health courses and how to read a cluster-points requirement.
kcse-subjects-and-cluster-points-for-hea.content:
Placement is not just about the mean grade. Many degree courses use cluster points based on specific subjects.

The idea

A cluster is a group of subjects relevant to a course. For competitive health courses reported in 2026, the cluster for medicine was said to involve mathematics, chemistry, biology and a language, and applicants are ranked by their cluster weight.

Why this matters

Two students with the same mean grade may have different cluster points. A strong biology and chemistry result is often more useful for health courses than a strong result in unrelated subjects.

How to use it

  • Check the course's required subjects on the official placement information.
  • Compare your cluster points with last year's cut-offs.
  • Choose a mixture of options.
  • Remember that diploma and certificate routes may have different requirements.

A caution

Formulas and cut-offs can change. Rely on official KUCCPS and institution notices.

Quick revision points

  • Cluster subjects matter, not just the mean grade.
  • Biology and chemistry are important for health courses.
  • Compare with past cut-offs, but expect change.
  • Choose a mix of options.
  • Rely on official notices.

knqa-and-recognition-of-qualifications-w.content:
The Kenya National Qualifications Authority (KNQA) was set up in 2015 to coordinate the quality assurance and comparability of qualifications.

What it does

According to its website, KNQA supports services such as recognition of prior learning, alignment and validation of qualifications and registration on the national qualifications database.

Why graduates should care

If you studied abroad, trained informally or want your qualification placed in the national framework, KNQA can be relevant. It also helps employers and institutions understand what level a qualification is.

What it is not

It does not replace professional regulators who license or register practitioners. You may need both.

Practical step

If you have questions about your certificate level or recognition, contact KNQA and ask for the current process.

Quick revision points

  • KNQA coordinates the national qualifications framework.
  • It supports alignment and recognition.
  • It does not replace professional regulators.

how-to-set-up-a-theatre-before-the-list-.title: How to set up a theatre before the list starts: a checklist
how-to-set-up-a-theatre-before-the-list-.excerpt: A practical checklist for preparing an operating theatre before the first case: room, equipment, trays and communication.
how-to-set-up-a-theatre-before-the-list-.content:
The first case of the day goes well or badly depending on what happened in the twenty minutes before it. Here is a structure that works for students.

1. Know the list

Read the operating list: patient names, procedures, side, surgeon, anaesthetist and any special equipment. Ask what is different today.

2. Check the room

  • Surfaces clean, floor dry, doors closed.
  • Temperature and ventilation as per policy.
  • Lights positioned and working.
  • Operating table working and positioned.
  • Suction, diathermy and any gas supply tested.

3. Supplies and sets

Check the sterile sets for integrity, indicators and expiry. Open what you need only when the patient is ready, according to local practice. Have extras of common items near but unopened.

4. Talk to the team

Introduce yourself, confirm the first case and ask if anything is needed. A thirty-second chat avoids a ten-minute delay.

5. Leave a note

Write what you found faulty and report it. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Read the list before you touch anything.
  • Test equipment before the patient arrives.
  • Check sterile packs for integrity and expiry.
  • Open supplies only when appropriate.
  • Report faults immediately.

theatre-turnover-between-cases-a-safe-an.title: Theatre turnover between cases: a safe and fast checklist
theatre-turnover-between-cases-a-safe-an.excerpt: How to turn a theatre over between patients without cutting corners on cleaning, counts or sharps.
theatre-turnover-between-cases-a-safe-an.content:
Turnover is a balance between speed and safety. Speed that skips cleaning is not efficiency.

Order matters

  • Make sure the patient has left safely and the count and documentation are complete.
  • Dispose of sharps first, then waste and linen in the correct bags.
  • Remove used instruments for decontamination according to policy.
  • Clean and disinfect the table, lights, trolleys and high-touch surfaces.
  • Clean floors as required.
  • Reset the table, suction and equipment for the next case.

Protect yourself

Wear appropriate PPE and avoid handling sharps with bare hands. Report any needle-stick or splash immediately.

Work as a team

Assign tasks quickly and speak up. One person cleaning while another prepares the next set reduces delay.

Do not skip

A faster turnover is never a reason to skip a step in cleaning or counting. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Sharps first, then waste and linen.
  • Clean high-touch surfaces every time.
  • Wear PPE during cleaning.
  • Share tasks and communicate.
  • Never trade safety for speed.

surgical-hand-scrub-how-it-works-and-com.title: Surgical hand scrub: how it works and common mistakes
surgical-hand-scrub-how-it-works-and-com.excerpt: The logic of the surgical scrub, from nails to elbows, and the mistakes students make most often.
surgical-hand-scrub-how-it-works-and-com.content:
The surgical scrub reduces the number of microorganisms on the hands and forearms before gloving. It is different from routine hand washing.

Before you scrub

Remove jewellery, trim nails, check skin for cuts, put on the cap, mask and eye protection. Avoid artificial nails.

The principle

Start from the cleanest area and keep hands higher than elbows so water flows from fingertips to elbows. Follow the time and method set by your hospital and the product's instructions, whether it is a traditional scrub with antiseptic soap or an alcohol-based surgical hand rub.

Common mistakes

  • Touching the tap or sink after scrubbing.
  • Letting hands drop below the waist.
  • Rushing the nails and between fingers.
  • Dripping water onto the gown.
  • Re-contaminating while drying.

Practise

Practise the sequence in front of a supervisor and ask for feedback. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Hands stay higher than elbows.
  • Follow your hospital's timing and product.
  • Nails and between fingers need attention.
  • Do not touch unsterile items after scrubbing.
  • Practise with feedback.

gowning-and-gloving-closed-and-open-tech.title: Gowning and gloving: closed and open technique explained
gowning-and-gloving-closed-and-open-tech.excerpt: What closed and open gloving mean, when each is used and how to avoid touching the outside of the glove with bare skin.
gowning-and-gloving-closed-and-open-tech.content:
Gowning and gloving look simple until you try with your hands inside long sleeves. A little understanding of the principle helps.

Closed technique

In closed gloving, your hands stay inside the gown sleeves until the glove is in place. This keeps bare skin from touching the outside of the glove and is the usual method for the scrubbed team.

Open technique

In open gloving, your hands are exposed and you take the glove by the inside of the cuff, then slide the second glove with gloved fingers under the cuff. It is used for quick tasks and where full gowning is not needed.

Key principles

  • Sterile touches sterile; unsterile touches unsterile.
  • Do not touch the outside of the glove with bare hands.
  • Check for holes; change gloves if torn or contaminated.
  • Keep hands above waist and below shoulders in the sterile zone.

Practise

Practise with a partner watching for contamination. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Closed technique keeps hands inside sleeves.
  • Open technique is for quick tasks.
  • Never touch the outside of the glove with bare skin.
  • Change gloves if torn or contaminated.
  • Practise with observation.

surgical-draping-basics-for-theatre-stud.title: Surgical draping basics for theatre students
surgical-draping-basics-for-theatre-stud.excerpt: Why we drape, how drapes create a sterile field and the principles behind placing them.
surgical-draping-basics-for-theatre-stud.content:
Draping turns a patient into a surgical field. A drape is only useful if it is placed once, correctly.

The purpose

Drapes create a sterile barrier between the surgical site and the rest of the patient and the room. They also protect equipment and define the working area.

Key principles

  • Drape after the skin prep has dried.
  • Place the drape from the near side to the far side, away from you, and avoid dragging it across unsterile areas.
  • Once placed, do not move a drape; a repositioned drape is contaminated.
  • Hold the drape by the folded edges and protect your gloved hands.

Types

There are towel drapes, fenestrated drapes, sheets and specialty drapes for different surgery. Reusable and disposable materials differ in how they are managed.

Ask and watch

Watch an experienced person drape, ask why each step is done and then practise. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Drape after prep is dry.
  • Place once; do not reposition.
  • Hold drapes by the folded edge.
  • Different surgery needs different drapes.
  • Learn by watching, then practising.

neutral-zone-and-safe-sharps-passing-in-.title: The neutral zone: passing sharps safely in theatre
neutral-zone-and-safe-sharps-passing-in-.excerpt: What the neutral zone is, why hand-to-hand passing of sharps causes injuries and how to apply the technique.
neutral-zone-and-safe-sharps-passing-in-.content:
Many sharps injuries happen during passing between people. A neutral zone is a simple way to prevent them.

The idea

A neutral zone is a designated area, such as a tray or a part of the field, where sharps are placed instead of being handed directly. The person passing puts the item down, and the person receiving picks it up.

Rules

  • Use a clear, agreed location.
  • Announce when you place a sharp.
  • Point the sharp away from people.
  • Load and unload blades with an instrument, not fingers.
  • Dispose of sharps in an approved container at the point of use.

Why it works

It removes the moment when two hands are near the same blade.

If an injury happens

Report immediately, follow your hospital's exposure protocol and seek assessment. Early reporting is part of safe practice. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Use a neutral zone for sharps.
  • Announce sharps when placing them.
  • Use instruments to load and unload blades.
  • Dispose of sharps immediately.
  • Report every injury straight away.
