instrument-passing-and-receiving-techniq.title: Instrument passing and receiving: technique for students
instrument-passing-and-receiving-techniq.excerpt: How to pass instruments so the surgeon receives them in a ready-to-use position, with tips for learning the rhythm of a case.
instrument-passing-and-receiving-techniq.content:
Passing instruments is a skill you can practise at home with spoons, pens and a cloth.

Principles

  • Pass instruments so the surgeon can use them without adjusting.
  • Place the handle into the palm firmly with a clear sense of contact.
  • Keep sharp tips away from hands.
  • Return used instruments to the Mayo stand in an organised way.
  • Keep the field tidy and counted.

Anticipation

The best scrub staff watch the surgical field and predict the next step. They learn this by studying the procedure beforehand and observing the surgeon's preferences.

Practise

Practise naming and passing instruments with a classmate. Start slowly and add speed only when accuracy is solid.

Communication

Use short, clear words. If you do not know what the surgeon asked for, ask, rather than guessing. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Pass so the instrument is ready to use.
  • Keep sharp tips away from people.
  • Anticipate by studying the procedure.
  • Practise names and passing.
  • Ask if unsure.

theatre-lights-and-equipment-basics-for-.title: Theatre lights and equipment basics for new students
theatre-lights-and-equipment-basics-for-.excerpt: A basic orientation to surgical lights, tables, diathermy units, suction and other equipment you will meet in an operating theatre.
theatre-lights-and-equipment-basics-for-.content:
On your first day the room looks like machines and cables. Learn what each is for and how to check it.

Surgical lights

Lights provide bright, shadow-reduced illumination. Learn how to position and adjust them and how to handle them without breaking sterility. Report flickering or heat issues.

Operating table

Tables can be raised, lowered, tilted and fitted with attachments. Learn the controls and how to lock them. Never move a table with a patient unless you are trained and the team agrees.

Suction and gases

Suction removes fluid and smoke from the field; check that canisters are secure, tubing is connected and suction pressure is working. Know where the emergency gas shut-offs are, as per your hospital.

Diathermy

Diathermy (electrosurgery) cuts and coagulates tissue using electric current. Follow the safety rules in my diathermy safety post and your hospital's protocol.

Reporting

Faulty equipment should be labelled and reported, not quietly set aside. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Learn the controls before the first case.
  • Do not move a table with a patient unless trained.
  • Check suction function and connections.
  • Know emergency shut-offs.
  • Label and report faulty equipment.

tourniquet-safety-basics-in-orthopaedic-.title: Tourniquet safety basics in limb surgery
tourniquet-safety-basics-in-orthopaedic-.excerpt: What a pneumatic tourniquet does, what to check and why recording the inflation time matters.
tourniquet-safety-basics-in-orthopaedic-.content:
A tourniquet lets the surgeon work in a nearly bloodless field, but it is not harmless.

Before use

Check the cuff for leaks, the tubing for kinks and the machine for a working display. Place a protective layer under the cuff, avoid wrinkles and protect the skin from prep solution.

During use

The surgeon or protocol sets the pressure. Record the time of inflation and tell the team at regular intervals as per local practice.

After use

Deflate only when the surgeon or anaesthetist says so and note the time. Check the skin underneath.

Risks

Too much pressure or too long a duration can injure nerves, skin and tissue. This is why timing and pressure matter. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Check the cuff and machine before use.
  • Protect skin under the cuff.
  • Record inflation time.
  • Pressure is set per surgeon and protocol.
  • Report skin or nerve concerns.

handling-surgical-specimens-labelling-an.title: Handling surgical specimens: labelling and safety
handling-surgical-specimens-labelling-an.excerpt: Why specimen handling errors are serious and how to label, store and transport specimens correctly.
handling-surgical-specimens-labelling-an.content:
A mislabelled specimen can lead to the wrong diagnosis for the wrong patient. It is a classic never-event.

Principles

  • Confirm with the surgeon what the specimen is and from where.
  • Label the container with the patient details and specimen type at the point of collection, following local rules.
  • Use the right container and preservative if required.
  • Record the specimen in the theatre register.
  • Transport safely and record who received it.

Safety

Treat specimens as potentially infectious. Wear gloves, avoid spills and clean spills quickly according to protocol.

Read back

A read-back between scrub and circulating staff reduces mistakes: say what the specimen is, say what is on the label, and confirm.

If in doubt

Ask the surgeon before the specimen leaves the room. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Label at the point of collection.
  • Read back specimen details aloud.
  • Use the correct container.
  • Record in the register.
  • Treat all specimens as infectious.

laparoscopic-surgery-basics-for-theatre-.title: Laparoscopic surgery basics for theatre students
laparoscopic-surgery-basics-for-theatre-.excerpt: What laparoscopic (keyhole) surgery involves, the equipment stack and why it needs extra checking.
laparoscopic-surgery-basics-for-theatre-.content:
Laparoscopy uses small incisions, a camera and long instruments. For the theatre team, it adds equipment and a different rhythm.

The equipment stack

The usual setup includes a camera and monitor, a light source, an insufflator for gas, suction and irrigation, and diathermy. Learn the connections and test them before the patient is brought in.

Differences from open surgery

  • The view is on a screen, so positioning of monitors matters.
  • Instruments are long and delicate; handle and clean them carefully.
  • Gas flow and pressure are monitored.
  • The team must be ready to convert to an open operation if needed.

Cleaning and care

Delicate scopes and instruments need correct cleaning and sterilisation as per manufacturer and hospital procedure.

Learn by watching

Ask to observe, ask for the equipment layout and learn to troubleshoot basic problems such as a fogging lens. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Test the equipment stack before the case.
  • Monitor position matters.
  • Be ready to convert to open surgery.
  • Handle scopes carefully.
  • Follow manufacturer and hospital cleaning rules.

caesarean-section-theatre-set-up-what-to.excerpt: A general overview of how a theatre team prepares for a caesarean section, including emergencies and neonatal readiness.
caesarean-section-theatre-set-up-what-to.content:
Caesarean sections are among the most common operations in many hospitals, and many are emergencies.

Preparation

The theatre should be ready quickly: table, lights, suction, diathermy, instruments and swabs. Local protocols decide exact sets and drugs.

The baby

A resuscitation area for the newborn should be prepared with warmth, suction and equipment as per hospital protocols, and a person assigned to receive the baby.

Counts and safety

Swabs, instruments and sharps are counted before and after the procedure, and the WHO checklist is used at the key pauses.

Teamwork

Because many caesareans are urgent, clear roles and calm communication matter. Know who is calling whom and where equipment is stored. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Be ready quickly but do not skip checks.
  • Prepare a resuscitation area for the newborn.
  • Count swabs, sharps and instruments.
  • Use the WHO checklist pauses.
  • Know the roles in an emergency.

orthopaedic-theatre-basics-power-tools-t.title: Orthopaedic theatre basics: power tools, trays and implants
orthopaedic-theatre-basics-power-tools-t.excerpt: An orientation to orthopaedic surgery from the theatre perspective: bone instruments, power equipment and implant handling.
orthopaedic-theatre-basics-power-tools-t.content:
Orthopaedic surgery is physical, noisy and equipment heavy. A new student should know what to expect.

Instruments and power tools

Bone surgery uses specialised instruments, drills, saws and sometimes saws with batteries or air power. These need correct assembly, cleaning and checking before use.

Implants

Implants such as plates, screws and joint components come in different sizes and sets. Check that the correct implant and size are available and recorded, and follow rules for opening only when needed.

Imaging

X-ray imaging may be used during the case. Follow radiation protection rules, including lead aprons and distance.

Ergonomics

Emergency cases feel different: faster, louder, less predictable. But the fundamentals do not change.

What stays the same

Asepsis, counts, communication and patient safety remain essential, even when time is short. The checklist still matters.

Before an emergency

Know where emergency sets, extra sutures, suction and blood warming equipment are stored. Practise setting up quickly.

In the moment

  • Listen for the plan and your role.
  • Do the basics first: room, sets, suction, diathermy.
  • Ask short, specific questions.
  • Do not hide mistakes; say so immediately.
  • Keep sharps and counts under control.

After

Debrief when the case ends: what worked, what did not, what to restock. Taking care of yourself matters too. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Fundamentals do not change in emergencies.
  • Know where emergency equipment is stored.
  • Do the basics first.

malignant-hyperthermia-awareness-for-the.title: Malignant hyperthermia: awareness for theatre staff
malignant-hyperthermia-awareness-for-the.excerpt: A rare but life-threatening anaesthetic reaction. What theatre staff should know to recognise and respond as a team.
malignant-hyperthermia-awareness-for-the.content:
Malignant hyperthermia (MH) is a rare inherited reaction to certain anaesthetic agents. It is an emergency requiring a rapid team response.

The basics

MH can be triggered by some volatile anaesthetic gases and a muscle relaxant used in anaesthesia. Signs can include a rapid rise in carbon dioxide on monitoring, fast heart rate, muscle rigidity and rising temperature. The anaesthetic team leads recognition and treatment.

What theatre staff do

  • Alert the team and help as directed.
  • Know where emergency drugs and cooling supplies are kept.
  • Be ready to assist with equipment, fluids and monitoring.
  • Follow the hospital's MH protocol.

Why awareness matters

In rare emergencies, minutes matter. If the whole team knows the plan, response is faster.

Note

This is awareness-level information. Learn your hospital's protocol and take part in drills. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • MH is rare but life-threatening.
  • The anaesthetic team leads treatment.
  • Know where emergency drugs are kept.
  • Practise the protocol in drills.
  • Speed and teamwork matter.

fire-safety-in-the-operating-theatre-the.title: Fire safety in the operating theatre: the fire triangle applied
fire-safety-in-the-operating-theatre-the.excerpt: Why fires can start in theatre and how oxygen, fuel and ignition sources come together, with practical prevention rules.
fire-safety-in-the-operating-theatre-the.content:
Operating theatres contain the three elements of fire in close proximity: oxygen, fuel and an ignition source.

The triangle

  • Oxidiser: oxygen or nitrous oxide-rich environments.
  • Fuel: drapes, gauze, alcohol-based prep, hair and some gases.
  • Ignition: diathermy, lasers, fibre-optic light sources and sparks.

Prevention

  • Allow alcohol-based skin preps to dry fully before draping and using diathermy.
  • Keep diathermy tips holstered when not in use.
  • Use moist swabs near oxygen-rich areas where appropriate.
  • Communicate between surgeon and anaesthetist when using ignition sources near oxygen.

Know your plan

Know the location of fire alarms, extinguishers and exits and how to turn off gases in an emergency. Practise drills.

In a fire

Follow your hospital's plan: rescue, alarm, contain, extinguish or evacuate. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Oxygen, fuel and ignition create fire risk.
  • Let alcohol preps dry.
  • Holster diathermy when not in use.
  • Communicate before using ignition near oxygen.
  • Know alarms, extinguishers and exits.

radiation-safety-in-theatre-time-distanc.content:
C-arm imaging is common in orthopaedic and some other surgery. Staff must protect themselves using simple principles.

Three basics

  • Time: reduce the time you are near the beam.
  • Distance: radiation drops quickly as you move away.
  • Shielding: wear lead aprons, thyroid collars and use shields where provided.

Practical steps

Wear a dosimeter if your hospital provides one and keep it where instructed. Store lead aprons hung, not folded, to avoid cracks. Announce 'X-ray' before exposures so everyone can step back.

Staff health

If you are or may be pregnant, tell your supervisor early so they can adjust your duties according to policy.

Radiation protection programme

Follow your hospital's radiation protection rules and training. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Use time, distance and shielding.
  • Wear lead aprons and collars.
  • Announce exposures aloud.
  • Store lead aprons properly.
  • Tell your supervisor if pregnant.

Your role as a student

Take your own allergies seriously

If you have glove or material allergies, tell your supervisor early. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

patient-identification-consent-and-site-.content:
Wrong-patient and wrong-site surgery are rare but devastating. Systems exist to prevent them, and every team member is part of that system.

Identity

Confirm the patient's name, age or number against the wristband, theatre list and chart, asking the patient where possible.

Procedure and site

Confirm the planned procedure and the side or site. Many hospitals mark the site before the patient comes to theatre. If it is not marked, ask.

Consent

Confirm that consent has been obtained according to hospital policy. Theatre staff do not obtain consent but should notice if it is missing.

Time-out

The WHO Surgical Safety Checklist includes a pause before incision where the team confirms patient, site and procedure together. Anyone can stop the process if something does not match. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Check identity against wristband and chart.
  • Confirm procedure, site and side.
  • Notice if consent is missing and raise it.

sterile-packs-indicators-and-expiry-what.title: Sterile packs, indicators and expiry: what to check before opening
sterile-packs-indicators-and-expiry-what.excerpt: What to check on a sterile pack before use: integrity, indicators, labels and storage.
sterile-packs-indicators-and-expiry-what.content:
A sterile item is only sterile if the packaging has remained intact. Here is what to check every time.

Before opening

  • Is the wrapping intact, with no holes, tears or stains?
  • Is the pack dry?
  • Does the chemical indicator show the expected change?
  • Is it within the expiry or event-related limit used by your hospital?
  • Is the label correct?

If a pack fails

Do not use it. Set it aside, label it and tell your supervisor or CSSD.

Storage

Sterile supplies should be stored in a clean, dry, controlled area, handled minimally and not stored on the floor.

Indicators

A chemical indicator shows the pack has been exposed to a process, but it does not by itself prove sterility. Biological indicators and process monitoring give more confidence. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Check integrity, dryness, indicator and date.
  • Do not use a pack that fails any check.
  • Store sterile items properly.
  • Indicators show exposure, not proof alone.
  • Report failures to CSSD.

cssd-workflow-from-dirty-to-sterile-and-.title: CSSD workflow: from dirty to sterile and back
cssd-workflow-from-dirty-to-sterile-and-.excerpt: How instruments travel through a central sterile services department, and why the one-way flow matters.
cssd-workflow-from-dirty-to-sterile-and-.content:
The CSSD is the engine room of safe surgery. Understanding it makes you a better theatre team member.

One-way flow

The flow goes from dirty to clean to sterile and never back. Staff, trolleys and air should not cross from dirty to clean areas.

Steps

  • Collection and transport of used instruments in closed containers.
  • Cleaning, which removes soil, and decontamination.
  • Inspection for damage and function.
  • Packing with indicators and labels.
  • Sterilisation by a validated method.
  • Storage and issue to theatre.

What you can do

Send instruments back promptly, remove gross soil as per policy, keep sharps contained and report damaged instruments.

Respect

CSSD staff protect every patient. A friendly word to them goes a long way. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Flow goes dirty to clean to sterile.
  • Cleaning must come before sterilisation.
  • Inspect instruments for damage.
  • Send instruments back promptly and safely.
  • Respect CSSD teams.

closed-loop-communication-and-escalation.title: Closed-loop communication and escalation in theatre
closed-loop-communication-and-escalation.excerpt: How to speak so messages are understood in a noisy theatre, and how to escalate concerns respectfully.
closed-loop-communication-and-escalation.content:
Most errors in healthcare involve communication. Closed-loop communication is simple and powerful.

The loop

  • The sender names the person and states the request.
  • The receiver repeats it back.
  • The sender confirms it is correct.
  • The receiver tells the sender when it is done.

Example

Surgeon: 'Nurse, please give me a 3-0 suture.' Nurse: '3-0 suture, passing now.' Surgeon: 'Thank you.' It takes seconds and prevents mistakes.

Escalating concerns

Use a clear, calm structure: say what you see, say why it concerns you, say what you need. If the first person does not respond and safety is at stake, escalate to a senior.

Culture

Teams that welcome questions are safer. Thank colleagues who speak up. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

Quick revision points

  • Name the person and state the request.
  • Repeat back and confirm.
  • Say what you see, why it matters, what you need.
  • Escalate if safety is at risk.
  • Thank people who speak up.

the-three-phases-of-perioperative-care-e.content:
The word perioperative covers the whole surgical journey, not just the time in the operating room.

Preoperative

Includes assessment, tests, consent, fasting instructions, medication review and preparation. Many errors begin here, so checks are important.

Intraoperative

From the patient's arrival in theatre to leaving it: anaesthesia, positioning, skin prep, surgery, counts and the safety checklist.

Postoperative

Includes recovery room care, pain control, monitoring and ward care. See my post on the recovery room.

Why the term matters

Perioperative theatre technology is named for this wider view: you are part of a chain of care where handovers matter. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

  • Perioperative means before, during and after surgery.
  • Preoperative checks prevent many errors.

Be reliable

Arrive early, wear your PPE correctly, keep your hands to yourself in the sterile field and own your mistakes.

back-and-body-care-for-theatre-staff-erg.content:
Theatre work is physical. A career of thirty years begins with how you treat your body in the first three.

Feet and legs

Wear supportive, closed, non-slip shoes that suit theatre rules. Move your weight and avoid locking your knees.

Back

Keep your back neutral when lifting. Use your legs and ask for help with heavy trays and patients. Use slide sheets and transfer equipment where available.

Breaks and hydration

Take breaks when the list allows, stretch, drink water and eat properly. Dehydration and hunger can reduce concentration.

Mind

Long lists are mentally tiring. Short pauses, good sleep and talking to a trusted person help. Always follow your own hospital's policy and your supervisor's instructions; this post is for learning, not a replacement for local protocols.

  • Good shoes matter.
  • Lift with your legs and ask for help.
  • Use transfer aids.

who-regulates-health-professions-in-keny.content:
Newcomers to health careers hear many acronyms. Think of them as answering different questions.

The main bodies

  • Kenya Medical Practitioners and Dentists Council (KMPDC): regulates medical practitioners and dentists under its Act.
  • Nursing Council of Kenya (NCK): regulates nursing and midwifery, including registration, licensing and licensing examinations.
  • Clinical Officers Council: regulates clinical officers.
  • Other boards cover areas such as pharmacy, laboratory, nutrition, physiotherapy and public health, each under its own law.
  • TVET Authority (TVETA) and the Commission for University Education (CUE) accredit institutions.
  • Kenya National Qualifications Authority (KNQA) coordinates the national qualifications framework.

Which question to ask whom

Is the college accredited? TVETA or CUE. Is the programme recognised for registration? The professional regulator. What level is my qualification? KNQA.

Where theatre technologists fit

Registration routes for some mid-level cadres have been discussed and changed over time. See my separate post on where theatre technologists register. Regulations and office-holders change, so confirm on the official website before acting on anything here.

Tip

Keep a folder with your certificates, transcripts, ID and any registration documents.

Quick revision points

  • Different bodies answer different questions.
  • Institutions are accredited by TVETA or CUE.
  • Professional councils register and license practitioners.
  • KNQA handles the qualifications framework.

health-regulators-merger-and-new-authori.content:
Several Kenyan outlets reported proposals to merge or restructure the bodies that regulate health professions, with a body referred to as the Kenya Health Professions Oversight Authority mentioned in coverage. I could not confirm the current legal status, so treat this as a reported plan, not a settled rule.

What is being discussed

The idea in the coverage is to reduce fragmentation by consolidating regulators or placing them under a single oversight body, with the aim of improving standards, discipline and registration processes. Details such as timelines, which councils are affected and transition rules were reported in different ways.

Why it matters to students

If regulators merge, registration routes and portals may change. Cadres without clear registration, which have been a recurring concern in the sector, may be clarified.

What not to do

Do not pay anyone who claims to have inside information on new registration. Do not assume old rules disappear overnight.

What to do

  • Follow your professional council's official notices.
  • Follow the Ministry of Health announcements.
  • Keep your documents in order.
  • Read the final law and transition notices when published.

Caution

I am summarising reports, not the law. Regulations and office-holders change, so confirm on the official website before acting on anything here.

Many places exist in some science and technical programmes, while medicine is intensely competitive. Strong science grades open options, and technical routes can perform well.

The Association of Surgical Technologists (AST) in the United States has student membership and local assemblies, and the Association of periOperative Registered Nurses (AORN) publishes guidelines and runs education programmes. They are not Kenyan regulators, and their guidelines are written for their own context, but they are respected sources of practice standards.

Ask your lecturers and senior colleagues about local associations, student bodies and county professional groups. Check that an association is registered and has real activities.

Be careful

Do not pay large fees to unknown groups. Ask for the constitution, officials and a record of activities.

  • Check legitimacy before paying.

how-to-spot-medical-misinformation-on-so.title: How to spot medical misinformation on social media
how-to-spot-medical-misinformation-on-so.excerpt: Seven quick checks for deciding whether a health post is reliable, for learners and for creators.
how-to-spot-medical-misinformation-on-so.content:
Misinformation spreads because it is simple and emotional. You can slow it down.

Checks

  • Who is the author, and what is their expertise?
  • Does the post cite a guideline or study, and can you find it?
  • How old is the information?
  • Does it promise a miracle or hide a sale?
  • Do reputable organisations such as the WHO or the Ministry of Health say the same?
  • Is it asking you to share urgently?
  • Does it ignore risks?

As a creator

Cite sources, correct mistakes and avoid dramatic claims. I wrote about making accurate medical content in another post.

What to do

Do not share unverified claims. If you know a post is wrong, comment politely with a source or report it.

Resource

The WHO publishes reliable information on many health topics.

Quick revision points

  • Check author, evidence and date.
  • Be wary of miracle claims.
  • Compare with reputable organisations.
  • Do not share unverified posts.
  • Correct mistakes politely.

how-to-start-a-theatre-technology-study-.excerpt: Steps for starting a small study club on campus or online, with ideas for activities and rules.
how-to-start-a-theatre-technology-study-.content:
A small group with a regular routine does more than a large group with no plan.

Steps

  • Write a one-sentence purpose, for example 'weekly revision for theatre technology students'.
  • Find two or three co-organisers.
  • Choose a regular time and place or a WhatsApp group.
  • Ask a lecturer to advise.
  • Agree rules: respect, privacy, no sharing of leaked exams.

Activities

Past paper practice, instrument name quizzes, skill demonstrations, guest talks from graduates and attachment experience sharing.

Grow gradually

Invite seniors to mentor and juniors to learn. Document what you do so the club survives after you graduate.

Check with your institution

Ask about policies for student groups and use of the college name.

Quick revision points

  • Start with a clear purpose.
  • Keep it small and regular.
  • Ask a lecturer to advise.
  • Agree rules for privacy and honesty.
  • Document so it lasts.

rules-for-sharing-theatre-photos-and-vid.title: Rules for sharing theatre photos and videos online
rules-for-sharing-theatre-photos-and-vid.excerpt: Patient privacy and hospital policy come before likes. What is and is not appropriate to post about your clinical work.
rules-for-sharing-theatre-photos-and-vid.content:
Training can feel exciting, and the temptation to post is real. A single careless photo can harm a patient and end a career.

Never post

  • Patients, their faces, bodies, records, wristbands or images that could identify them.
  • Photos or videos from inside theatre unless your institution has clear written permission.
  • Anything that shows colleagues without their consent.
  • Screens, charts or lists with names.

Safer ways to share

Use models, drawings, empty rooms with permission, equipment from teaching labs and your own study notes.

Rules of thumb

If in doubt, do not post. Ask your supervisor or the communications office. Remember that deleted posts can still be saved by others.

Professionalism

Employers and regulators look at what you post. Your online behaviour is part of your professional reputation.

Quick revision points

  • Never post anything that could identify a patient.
  • Follow hospital policy.
  • Use models and drawings.
  • Ask first if unsure.
  • Your posts shape your reputation.

hashtags-and-search-terms-for-finding-th.content:
Finding good content is easier when you know the words people use.

Terms to try

  • perioperative theatre technology
  • operating theatre, operating room
  • surgical technologist, scrub nurse (a different role, but related content)
  • sterile field, aseptic technique
  • surgical instruments, CSSD
  • medical students Kenya, health students Kenya
  • anatomy mnemonics, medical terminology

Tagging your own posts

Use a few accurate tags rather than dozens. Mix broad and specific ones. Add your location or college if appropriate.

Searching smartly

Combine words, check the newest posts and look at who is commenting. Follow accounts that cite sources.

Remember

Hashtags help discovery, but content quality builds trust.

Quick revision points

  • Use several name variants when searching.
  • Combine topic and location words.
  • Use a few accurate tags.
  • Follow accounts that cite sources.
  • Quality builds trust.

finding-a-mentor-in-the-theatre-technolo.title: Finding a mentor in the theatre technology community
finding-a-mentor-in-the-theatre-technolo.excerpt: A respectful way to find and approach a mentor, and what to offer in return.
finding-a-mentor-in-the-theatre-technolo.content:
Many students are afraid to ask. Most professionals remember what it was like to start.

Where to look

Your lecturers, attachment supervisors, senior graduates, professional associations and professionals active on LinkedIn or in respectful online groups.

How to approach

  • Write a short message: who you are, what you admire, one specific question.
  • Offer a clear request, for example fifteen minutes by phone.
  • Be flexible and thank them.
  • Follow up with what you did with the advice.

What to offer

Reliability, curiosity and help where you can, such as designing a poster, sharing notes or helping with a small project.

Keep boundaries

Mentors give advice, not jobs or money. Do not pressure them. And never share personal or financial information with strangers online.

Quick revision points

  • Ask a specific, small question.
  • Be respectful of time.
  • Follow up with results.
  • Offer help in return.
  • Mentors advise; they do not owe you a job.
